Names are Wallace's and are not normalized: curly quotes, Greek headwords and parenthetical alternatives all occur.

nominative/primary-uses/subject.formation: A nominative naming who or what the verb's statement is about: the doer with an active verb, the one acted on with a passive. It agrees with its finite verb in number, and may be a noun, an adjective or participle used as a noun, or left unexpressed in the verb's ending.

nominative/primary-uses/predicate-nomina.description: approximately same as subject; can be in convertible or subset propositions
nominative/primary-uses/predicate-nomina.formation: A second nominative joined to the subject by a linking verb (εἰμί, γίνομαι, ὑπάρχω, or a passive such as εὑρίσκομαι or καλοῦμαι), saying what the subject is or becomes. The subject is the known term, a pronoun, an articular noun or a name; the predicate usually lacks the article and names the larger class.

nominative/primary-uses/nominative-simpl.description: two adjacent substantives that refer to the same thing/person
nominative/primary-uses/nominative-simpl.formation: A nominative noun set beside another nominative and naming the same person or thing a second way: 'the steward, a freedman'. It shares the first noun's role and often has the article; no verb joins them, as one would join a predicate nominative.

nominative/grammatically-independent-use.display_name: Grammatically Independent Uses of the Nominative

nominative/grammatically-independent-use.formation: A nominative standing outside any sentence, in introductory matter: the title of a book or section, the sender and addressee of a letter, a greeting. It has no verb, and none needs supplying.

nominative/grammatically-independent-use.description: logical rather than syntactical subject at beginning of a sentence
nominative/grammatically-independent-use.formation: A nominative set at the head of a sentence as its topic, after which the sentence continues in other syntax and picks the topic up with a pronoun in the case its own clause needs: 'the one who stays: I will reward him'. Often a substantival participle; it throws the topic forward for emphasis.

nominative/grammatically-independent-use.description: subject of an explanatory clause within another clause
nominative/grammatically-independent-use.formation: A nominative that is the subject of a brief explanatory clause set inside another sentence, an aside: 'a man came (his name was …)'. It does not head the sentence and interrupts its flow.

nominative/grammatically-independent-use.description: in proverbial expressions that have no finite verb

nominative/grammatically-independent-use.formation: A nominative, usually with the article, used to address someone in place of the vocative: 'ὁ διδάσκαλος' for 'teacher!'. The article marks it, since a vocative never takes one; it is common in the plural, where the two cases look alike.

nominative/grammatically-independent-use.description: exclamation without grammatical connection to rest of sentence

nominative/nominatives-place-oblique-cas.display_name: Nominatives in Place of Oblique Cases

nominative/nominatives-place-oblique-cas.description: a title that functions like a proper name, as if in quotes

nominative/nominatives-place-oblique-cas.display_name: Nominative in Apposition to Oblique Cases

nominative/nominatives-place-oblique-cas.description: ἀπὸ ὁ ὤν in Rev 1:4 only

vocative/direct-address/simple-address.formation: The vocative naming the one spoken to, without ὦ: 'daughter', 'lord', 'physician'. It usually stands near the front of its clause, set off by commas, as ordinary address whatever feeling the context lends it. Only singular masculine and feminine nouns show a distinct vocative ending.

vocative/direct-address/emphatic-emotion.formation: The vocative preceded by ὦ: 'O woman', 'O man'. In Koine ὦ marks strong feeling (rebuke, wonder, reproach), except in the more literary style of Acts, where it can be merely polite.

vocative/apposition.description: Two adjacent substantives that refer to the same thing/person

genitive/adjectival/descriptive-genitive.formation: A genitive noun, usually after its head noun, that characterizes the head: 'marked by', 'having to do with'. It is the default reading, left when nothing narrower fits: the head is not a verbal noun, does not belong to the genitive, is not a part of it, and the genitive cannot simply become an adjective on the head.

genitive/adjectival/possessive-genitive.formation: A genitive naming the owner of the head noun: 'belonging to'. The genitive is personal, and the head is something that can be owned (a possession, a servant, a house), not an abstract idea. A genitive personal pronoun (μου, αὐτοῦ) is its commonest form.

genitive/adjectival/genitive-relationshi.formation: A genitive naming the relative of the person the head noun names, after a noun of kinship (son, mother, brother, father). The genitive is personal. The kinship noun is often left out and only its article kept, leaving 'the [son] of' to be understood from the article's gender.

genitive/adjectival/partitive-genitive-w.description: denotes the whole of which the head noun is a part—which is a part of
genitive/adjectival/partitive-genitive-w.formation: A genitive naming the whole of which the head is a part: 'some of', 'one of', 'a third of'. The head is a word of portion or number (τις, εἷς, ἕκαστος, λοιπός, a fraction or ordinal), and the genitive is usually a plural group or a whole thing.

genitive/adjectival/attributive-genitive.description: specifies an attribute or innate quality of the head substantive; convert genitive into an attributive adjective
genitive/adjectival/attributive-genitive.formation: A genitive noun naming a quality of its head, so that it could be turned into an adjective on the head: 'a man of honour' is 'an honourable man'. The genitive is an abstract noun; the construction is more emphatic than the adjective would be, and the genitive takes no modifier of its own.

genitive/adjectival/attributed-genitive.description: semantically opposite of attributive genitive; convert head noun into adjective modifying the genitive noun
genitive/adjectival/attributed-genitive.formation: The reverse of the attributive genitive: the head noun names the quality and the genitive the thing that has it, so the head could be turned into an adjective on the genitive: 'the sweetness of the wine' is 'sweet wine'. The head is an abstract noun of quality or result.

genitive/adjectival/genitive-content.description: full of, containing (related to noun or verb)
genitive/adjectival/genitive-content.formation: A genitive naming what fills or is held in the word it depends on: after a verb of filling (πίμπλημι, πληρόω, γεμίζω), an adjective of fullness (πλήρης, μεστός), or a noun for a container (a net, a jar). After a verb of filling the content stands in the genitive, not the dative.

genitive/adjectival/genitive-simple-appo.description: genitive substantive adjacent to another genitive substantive, referring to the same thing/person—namely, which is
genitive/adjectival/genitive-simple-appo.formation: A genitive noun set beside another genitive noun and naming the same person or thing by a second designation: 'the merchant, his brother'. Both nouns share the case; the second often has the article. Unlike the genitive of apposition, 'of' cannot stand between them.

genitive/adjectival/genitive-apposition-.description: genitive states a specific example of which the head noun names a category—namely, which is

genitive/adjectival/genitive-destination.display_name: Genitive of Destination (a.k.a. Direction or Purpose)
genitive/adjectival/genitive-destination.description: for the purpose of, destined for, toward, or into

genitive/adjectival/predicate-genitive.description: simple apposition in genitive case made emphatic by participial form of the equative verb

genitive/adjectival/genitive-subordinati.description: specifies that which is subordinated to or under the dominion of the head noun—over

genitive/adjectival/genitive-production-.description: genitive produces the noun to which it stands related—produced by

genitive/adjectival/genitive-product.description: genitive is the product of the noun to which it stands related—which produces

genitive/ablatival-genitive/genitive-sep.description: genitive indicates that from which the verb or sometimes head noun is separated—out of, away from, or from
genitive/ablatival-genitive/genitive-sep.formation: A bare genitive, with no preposition, naming that from which something is separated, after a verb of leaving, abstaining, ceasing or removing (ἀφίστημι, ἀπέχομαι, παύομαι). The verb carries the separation; Koine usually spells the same idea with ἀπό or ἐκ, so the bare genitive belongs with such verbs.

genitive/ablatival-genitive/genitive-sou.description: the source from which the head noun derives or depends—out of, derived from, dependent on, or “sourced in”
genitive/ablatival-genitive/genitive-sou.formation: A genitive naming where the head noun comes from or what it depends on: 'from', 'derived from'. Koine usually says ἐκ with the genitive, so the bare genitive reads as source only where the context points to origin and neither possession nor a subjective genitive gives the sense.

genitive/ablatival-genitive/genitive-com.description: genitive after a comparative adjective, translated than

genitive/verbal-genitive-i-e-genitive-re.display_name: Verbal Genitive (i.e., Genitive Related to a Verbal Noun)

genitive/verbal-genitive-i-e-genitive-re.description: functions as subject of verbal idea implicit in head noun
genitive/verbal-genitive-i-e-genitive-re.formation: A genitive after a verbal noun (a noun with a cognate verb: testimony, coming, obedience, will) naming the one who does the action: 'the testimony of the witnesses' is 'the witnesses testify'. The implied verb may be transitive or not; the context must make the genitive the doer, not the one acted on.

genitive/verbal-genitive-i-e-genitive-re.description: functions as direct object of verbal idea implicit in head noun
genitive/verbal-genitive-i-e-genitive-re.formation: A genitive after a verbal noun naming what receives the action: 'faith in', 'love for', 'the building of the wall' ('someone builds the wall'). The implied verb must be transitive, and the doer is left to the context.

genitive/verbal-genitive-i-e-genitive-re.description: both subjective and objective (e.g., “Revelation of Jesus Christ” = “revelation about and from Jesus Christ”)

genitive/adverbial-genitive/genitive-pri.display_name: Genitive of Price or Value or Quantity
genitive/adverbial-genitive/genitive-pri.description: the price paid for the word to which it is related—for

genitive/adverbial-genitive/genitive-tim.formation: A noun of time in the genitive, usually without the article or a preposition, beside a verb: 'by night', 'during the day'. It names the kind of time the action falls within, where the dative gives a point in time and the accusative a stretch of it.

genitive/adverbial-genitive/genitive-pla.display_name: Genitive of Place (where or within which)
genitive/adverbial-genitive/genitive-pla.description: the place within which the verb to which it is related occurs

genitive/adverbial-genitive/genitive-mea.description: the means by which the verbal action is accomplished—by

genitive/adverbial-genitive/genitive-age.description: the personal agent by whom the action in view is accomplished; related to—τος adjective; by

genitive/adverbial-genitive/genitive-ass.formation: A genitive naming the one someone is joined with, after a noun of fellowship: most often a compound in συν- (fellow-servant, fellow-worker), or κοινωνός and μέτοχος. The genitive is personal, very often a pronoun: 'a fellow-servant with you'.

genitive/after-certain-words/genitive-af.display_name: Genitive After Certain Verbs (as a Direct Object)
genitive/after-certain-words/genitive-af.description: especially after verbs of sensation, emotion/volition, sharing, ruling
certain adjectives (such as ἄξιος, “worthy [of]”) and adverbs normally take a genitive “object”
occurs after certain nouns whose lexical nature requires a genitive
certain prepositions take the genitive after them (see chapter on prepositions)
genitive/after-certain-words/genitive-af.formation: A substantive in the genitive after a preposition that takes it (ἐκ, ἀπό, διά, περί, μετά, ὑπό, κατά, ὑπέρ). The preposition, not the case, carries the sense, so the phrase means what that preposition means with the genitive; ἐκ and ἀπό take no other case.

dative/pure-dative-uses/dative-indirect-.description: dative noun is that to or for which the action of a transitive verb is performed—to, for
dative/pure-dative-uses/dative-indirect-.formation: A dative, usually a person, that receives the direct object of a transitive verb, or the subject of a passive one: the one something is given, said, shown or sent to. Commonest with verbs of giving and speaking, with the thing given or said in the accusative beside it.

dative/pure-dative-uses/dative-interest-.display_name: Dative of Interest (including Advantage [commodi] and Disadvantage [incommodi])

dative/pure-dative-uses/dative-interest-.description: for the benefit of or in the interest of
dative/pure-dative-uses/dative-interest-.formation: A dative, usually personal, naming the one an action is done for or benefits: 'for you', 'for himself'. Often a personal or reflexive pronoun, after a verb whose sense makes the benefit the point (storing up, preparing, being profitable).

dative/pure-dative-uses/dative-interest-.description: for/unto the detriment of or to the disadvantage of or against
dative/pure-dative-uses/dative-interest-.formation: A dative, usually personal, naming the one an action tells against: 'against yourselves', 'to his harm'. Often a personal or reflexive pronoun, after a verb whose outcome counts against that person (testifying, bringing judgment, a gesture of rejection).

A dative, usually personal, naming the one whose interest the action touches: for someone's benefit (advantage) or against them (disadvantage). It often overlaps an indirect object, and is interest where the benefit or harm is what the sentence stresses; the verb's sense usually shows which.

dative/pure-dative-uses/dative-reference.formation: A dative, usually a thing, that limits a verb or adjective to one frame of reference: 'strong in body', 'poor in goods'. Without it the statement would not hold, or would say too much. It relates the subject to the dative from outside, where the dative of sphere places the subject within it.

dative/pure-dative-uses/ethical-dative.description: the person whose feelings or viewpoint are intimately tied to the action—as far as I am concerned, in my opinion

dative/pure-dative-uses/dative-destinati.description: the “to” idea when a nontransitive verb is used

dative/pure-dative-uses/dative-recipient.description: would be an indirect object, but it appears in verbless constructions (such as in titles and salutations)

dative/pure-dative-uses/dative-possessio.description: that to which the subject of an equative verb belongs—belonging to

dative/pure-dative-uses/predicate-dative.description: simple apposition in dative case made emphatic by participial form of the equative verb

dative/pure-dative-uses/dative-simple-ap.description: dative substantive adjacent to another dative substantive, referring to the same thing/person
dative/pure-dative-uses/dative-simple-ap.formation: A dative noun set beside another dative noun and naming the same person or thing a second way: 'to the merchant, his neighbour'. The second shares the first's role in the clause and often has the article.

dative/local-dative-uses/dative-place.description: see dative of sphere (with which it is combined)

dative/local-dative-uses/dative-sphere.description: the sphere or realm in which the word to which the dative is related takes place or exists—in the sphere of
dative/local-dative-uses/dative-sphere.formation: A dative, often a part of the inner person or the body (heart, spirit, flesh), naming the realm in which the verb's action or state takes place: 'troubled in spirit', 'weary in body'. It places the subject within that realm; the grammars often read the same dative as reference, and the two shade into each other.

dative/local-dative-uses/dative-time-whe.description: the time when the action of the main verb is accomplished—usually a point in time
dative/local-dative-uses/dative-time-whe.formation: A noun of time in the dative, usually with the article and often an ordinal or demonstrative, answering 'when?': the point at which the action falls ('on the sabbath', 'at that hour'). The genitive gives the kind of time and the accusative its extent; Koine often puts ἐν before this dative.

dative/local-dative-uses/dative-rule.description: the standard of conduct to which a person conforms—according to, or in conformity with

dative/instrumental-dative-uses/dative-a.description: the person or thing one associates with or accompanies—in association with
dative/instrumental-dative-uses/dative-a.formation: A dative naming the person one acts together with, after a verb compounded with συν- (eat with, rejoice with, travel with) or one whose sense is joint action. The dative is personal, very often a pronoun; it is the verbal counterpart of the genitive of association.

dative/instrumental-dative-uses/dative-m.description: the manner in which the action of the verb is accomplished (answering “How?”)—with, in
the means or instrument by which the verbal action is accomplished—by means of, with
dative/instrumental-dative-uses/dative-m.formation: A dative, usually a concrete and impersonal noun, naming the instrument or means by which the verb's action is done: 'with a sword', 'by a word', 'by boat'. It answers 'how?' and implies someone using it; a personal agent is expressed with ὑπό and the genitive instead.

dative/instrumental-dative-uses/dative-a.description: the personal agent by whom the action of the (passive) verb is accomplished—by

dative/instrumental-dative-uses/dative-m.description: by before a quantitative word in the dative (typically, πολλῷ [dative] + μᾶλλον)

dative/instrumental-dative-uses/dative-c.description: the cause or basis of the action of the verb—because of, on the basis of
dative/instrumental-dative-uses/dative-c.formation: A dative, usually an abstract noun, naming the reason or ground of the action: 'because of hunger', 'because of unbelief'. It answers 'why?' where means answers 'how?': the cause is not a tool that anyone uses.

dative/instrumental-dative-uses/cognate-.description: cognate to the verb either formally or conceptually; translate like an adverb

dative/instrumental-dative-uses/dative-m.description: the material that is used to accomplish the action of the verb; a quantitative word—“I write with pen (means) and ink (material)”

dative/instrumental-dative-uses/dative-c.description: the content that is used by a verb of filling—with

dative/dative-after-certain-words/dative.description: dative direct object, often involving personal relationship
dative/dative-after-certain-words/dative.formation: A dative that completes a verb as its object, after verbs of personal relation: trusting (πιστεύω), obeying (ὑπακούω), serving (δουλεύω, διακονέω), worshipping (προσκυνέω), thanking (εὐχαριστέω), following (ἀκολουθέω). The object is usually a person.

dative/dative-after-certain-words/dative.description: after a verbal noun; personal interest usually present; dative often corresponds to direct object—“service to the saints” = “serve the saints”
several adjectives take a dative; personal relation usually involved; no set pattern of translation
certain prepositions take a dative (see chapter on prepositions)
dative/dative-after-certain-words/dative.formation: A substantive in the dative after a preposition that takes it: ἐν and σύν take only the dative; ἐπί, παρά and πρός take it for position ('on', 'beside', 'at'). The preposition, not the case, carries the sense.

accusative/substantival-uses-accusative/.description: the immediate object of the action of a transitive verb
accusative/substantival-uses-accusative/.formation: The accusative naming what directly receives the action of a transitive verb, participle or infinitive. It is the normal case of an object; a genitive or dative object is due to the verb's own sense.

accusative/substantival-uses-accusative/.description: certain verbs take two direct objects, one a person and the other a thing (e.g., teaching, anointing, asking [“I teach you Greek”])
accusative/substantival-uses-accusative/.formation: Two accusatives after a verb of teaching, reminding, asking, clothing or giving to drink: one names the person affected, the other the thing: 'teach you all things', 'ask you one thing'. The person stands where a dative indirect object might otherwise be.

accusative/substantival-uses-accusative/.description: one accusative is the object, the other is its complement; equivalent to subject-predicate nominative (“I call him lord”)
accusative/substantival-uses-accusative/.formation: Two accusatives after a verb of making, calling, appointing, sending or regarding, the second saying what the first is made, called or taken to be: 'call you friends', 'make me well'. They are an embedded subject and predicate: the object is the pronoun, articular noun or name; the complement, often anarthrous, may come first for emphasis.

A verb taking two accusatives: either a person and a thing (teach, ask, clothe, give to drink), or an object and a complement saying what the object is made, called or regarded as (make, call, appoint, consider).

accusative/substantival-uses-accusative/.description: direct object that shares lexically or conceptually the idea of the verb (“do not treasure treasures”)
simple apposition made emphatic by a copula in participial form or infinitival form (an accusative related to subject of infinitive)
accusative of reference that functions like subject of infinitive (“I want you to know”)
accusative/substantival-uses-accusative/.formation: An accusative naming who does the action of an infinitive when that is not the main verb's subject: 'I want you to know', 'you must go'. It follows verbs of wishing, allowing and commanding, and δεῖ, and stands inside articular infinitive phrases; with a second accusative, the subject normally comes first.

accusative/substantival-uses-accusative/.description: the accusative of thing in a double accusative person-thing construction with an active verb retains its case when the verb is put in the passive (“I taught you the lesson” becomes “You were taught the lesson by me”)

accusative thrown forward to the beginning of the clause, followed by a sentence in which it is replaced by a pronoun in the case required by the syntax—with reference to (subset of acc. of reference)
accusative substantive adjacent to another accusative substantive, referring to the same thing/person
accusative/substantival-uses-accusative/.formation: An accusative noun set beside another accusative and naming the same person or thing a second way: 'a man, a stranger'. It shares the first noun's role, usually the object, and adds a clarifying designation.

accusative/adverbial-uses-accusative/adv.description: qualifies the action of the verb rather than indicating quantity or extent of the verbal action (δωρεάν is most frequent—freely)

accusative/adverbial-uses-accusative/acc.display_name: Accusative of Measure (or Extent of Space or Time)
accusative/adverbial-uses-accusative/acc.description: for the extent of, for the duration of (rare with space, common with time)
accusative/adverbial-uses-accusative/acc.formation: An accusative of a time or distance word, usually with a number or quantifier, telling how long or how far the action extends: 'for many days', 'a day's journey'. It answers 'how long?' or 'how far?', where the genitive gives the kind of time and the dative a point in it.

accusative/adverbial-uses-accusative/acc.description: restricts the reference of the verbal action—with reference to
the person or thing by whom or by which one swears an oath

accusative/accusative-after-certain-prep.description: Certain prepositions take the accusative after them

article.description: basically a conceptualizer & identifier, not a definitizer

article/regular-uses-article/as-pronoun-.description: functions as third person pronoun in nominative in μὲν … δέ construction or with δέ alone
article/regular-uses-article/as-pronoun-.formation: The nominative article standing alone, with no noun, followed by δέ (or μέν, μὲν οὖν) and then a finite verb or an adverbial participle: ὁ δέ, ἡ δέ, οἱ δέ. It stands for a third-person pronoun ('he', 'she', 'they') and refers to someone already present in the narrative, while δέ marks a change of subject, most often to the other party in an exchange of words. A participle after it is adverbial, since the article does not modify it.

article/regular-uses-article/as-pronoun-.description: who is, which is (the article with second and third attributive positions in which the modifier is not an adjective)
article/regular-uses-article/as-pronoun-.formation: An article repeated after an articular noun, or set after an anarthrous one, to introduce a modifier that is not an adjective: a participle, a prepositional phrase or a genitive. The second article agrees with the noun in gender, number and case, and English renders it 'who is', 'which is'. It is still the article, bound to its noun and pointing back to it; it gives the modifier emphasis or clarity, and could be dropped without changing the basic sense.

article/regular-uses-article/as-pronoun-.description: his, her (used in contexts in which possession is implied)
article/regular-uses-article/as-pronoun-.formation: The article alone, with no possessive pronoun or genitive, on a noun whose owner is plain from the context: a part of the body, a member of the family, one's own belongings. The owner is normally the subject of the clause, and English supplies 'his', 'her', 'their'. Without the article or a possessive pronoun, no possession is implied.

article/regular-uses-article/substantive.description: distinguishes one individual from another (“drip-pan” category)
article/regular-uses-article/substantive.formation: The article on a noun that singles out one particular thing or person from others of its kind where no narrower reason applies: it has not been mentioned before and is not unique, famous or the best of its class, but is simply the one that belongs to the situation, such as the stand in the room or the roof of the house. It is the category of last resort among the individualizing uses.

article/regular-uses-article/substantive.description: points out something mentioned earlier in the text, by way of reminder
article/regular-uses-article/substantive.formation: The article on a noun that has already been introduced, pointing back to that earlier mention: 'the — just mentioned'. The first mention is usually anarthrous, since it merely introduces the thing; later mentions take the article. The earlier mention may use a synonym, or even a verb of the same idea, and should stand in the near context.

article/regular-uses-article/substantive.description: points to something in the text that immediately follows
points out an object or person which/who is present at the moment of speaking; demonstrative force—this
article/regular-uses-article/substantive.formation: The article pointing to a person or thing physically present when the words are spoken, with the force of a demonstrative: 'this —', 'the — here'. It belongs in direct speech, where the speaker can point; Koine more often uses οὗτος for the same job.

article/regular-uses-article/substantive.description: object is “in a class by itself”
article/regular-uses-article/substantive.formation: The article marking a noun as the one member of its class that most deserves the name, although others share it: 'the — above all others'. It picks out the extreme of the class, the worst as readily as the best, and usually stands without a modifier; the context must show why this one stands out.

article/regular-uses-article/substantive.display_name: Monadic (“One of a Kind” or “Unique” Article)
article/regular-uses-article/substantive.formation: The article with a noun naming something of which there is only one, such as the sun, the moon, the earth or the sky. It does not set its noun apart from others of the kind, since there are none. A noun made unique by its modifier (an adjective or a genitive) works the same way, so the whole phrase is what counts.

article/regular-uses-article/substantive.description: well known, but for reasons other than the above categories; that which is familiar to the readers
article/regular-uses-article/substantive.formation: The article marking a person or thing as familiar to the readers for reasons outside the text: not mentioned before, not present, not unique and not the best of its class, but already known to them, such as 'the friends' or 'the elder' in a letter between people who share acquaintances and customs.

article/regular-uses-article/substantive.display_name: Abstract (i.e., the Article with Abstract Nouns)
article/regular-uses-article/substantive.description: identifies a quality or abstract concept (e.g., love, salvation, peace, faith); article is rarely used in translation
article/regular-uses-article/substantive.formation: The article with an abstract noun (love, wisdom, nature, truth), narrowing the quality to a particular instance or aspect of it: the love under discussion, the wisdom a speaker shows. English usually leaves the article untranslated. Articular abstract nouns are more common than anarthrous ones.

The article set before a noun and agreeing with it in gender, number and case, marking it off in one of two ways: as a particular individual distinguished from others of its kind (the individualizing article: already mentioned, present, unique, well known, or the best of its kind), or as a whole class distinguished from other classes (the generic article, 'as a class'). A noun with the article is always definite.

article/regular-uses-article/as-substant.display_name: As a Substantiver (With Certain Parts of Speech)
article/regular-uses-article/as-substant.description: Turns another part of speech into a substantive; conceptualizes the idea of that part of speech

article/regular-uses-article/as-substant.formation: The article placed before a participle, turning it into a noun: 'the one who —', 'those who —', 'the thing that —'. The article's gender, number and case give the participle its role in the sentence, while the participle keeps its tense and can take its own object and modifiers. It may name a particular person or a whole class of people who do the action.

The neuter singular article (τό, τοῦ, τῷ) placed before an infinitive to make it a noun, standing as subject or object, or as a genitive after a noun: 'to —', 'the —ing'. The article's case shows the infinitive's role, and the infinitive can still take its own object and an accusative subject. This is distinct from the articular infinitive after a preposition or expressing purpose.

An article with no noun of its own, set before a genitive word or phrase. The genitive does not agree with it; the article turns the whole into a noun whose gender supplies what is meant: the neuter plural 'the things of —' (affairs, interests), the masculine plural 'the people of —'. The article's case gives the phrase its role in the sentence.

article/regular-uses-article/as-function.display_name: As a Function Marker (often has semantic force as well; see categories above)

article/regular-uses-article/as-function.description: especially to denote the second attributive position (without separate semantic weight)
article/regular-uses-article/as-function.formation: The article marking an adjective as attributive when it follows its noun: repeated before both (article–noun–article–adjective, the second attributive position), or set only before the adjective after an anarthrous noun (the third attributive position). The second article adds almost no meaning of its own; it binds the adjective to the noun as a modifier, where an adjective outside the article-noun group would be predicate.

article/regular-uses-article/as-function.description: when αὐτοῦ and the like are attached to a noun, the article is almost invariably found as well
both the head noun and the genitive noun normally have or lack the article (Apollonius’ Canon)
article indicates the case of the noun
article/regular-uses-article/as-function.formation: The article used with a noun that does not decline, so that the article's case shows the noun's role in the sentence: subject, object, a genitive after another noun, or an indirect object. Without the article the reader could not tell which role the noun plays.

article/regular-uses-article/as-function.description: to denote substantival (or adjectival) function of the participle
a demonstrative in predicate position to an articular noun has an attributive relation; demonstratives do not modify anarthrous nouns
article/regular-uses-article/as-function.formation: A demonstrative (οὗτος, ἐκεῖνος) in predicate position to an articular noun, before the article or after the noun, which is how a demonstrative modifies a noun: 'this —', 'that —'. It never stands between the article and its noun. Beside an anarthrous noun a demonstrative is not attributive but a pronoun on its own.

article/regular-uses-article/as-function.display_name: To Distinguish Subject from Predicate Nominative and Object from Complement
article/regular-uses-article/as-function.description: subject/object have the article so as to distinguish them from PN/complement

article/regular-uses-article/as-function.display_name: With the Infinitive to Denote Various Functions

article/absence-article.description: may be indefinite, qualitative, or definite

article/absence-article/indefinite.description: Refers to one member of a class, without specifying which member; lacks referential identity

article/absence-article/qualitative.description: Stresses quality, nature, or essence; focuses on class traits

article/absence-article/definite.description: Stresses individual identity; has unique referential identity

article/absence-article/definite/proper-.description: definite with or without the article
article/absence-article/definite/proper-.formation: A proper name without the article, definite all the same, since a name already identifies what it names: a city's name means that city, not one of several. The article may or may not stand with a name, and its absence says nothing about definiteness; it simply names the person or place.

article/absence-article/definite/object-.description: object can be definite, qualitative, or indefinite
article/absence-article/definite/object-.formation: A noun after a preposition without the article yet definite, as in 'at home', 'in town', 'from the country': the preposition makes the article unnecessary. Such objects are often places or times. An anarthrous prepositional object may also be qualitative or indefinite, so the context decides.

article/absence-article/definite/ordinal.description: number specifies amount of substantive, making it definite
article/absence-article/definite/ordinal.formation: A noun with an ordinal number (first, third, sixth) but no article, definite because the number itself picks out which one: 'at the fourth watch', 'it was the sixth hour'. Common with the hours of the day and the watches of the night.

article/absence-article/definite/predica.description: if PN precedes copula, it may be definite
article/absence-article/definite/predica.formation: A predicate nominative without the article that stands before the linking verb (εἰμί, γίνομαι) and is definite from the context, often through a genitive of its own: 'this is the owner of the field'. Before the verb a definite predicate usually drops the article; the subject keeps it, or is a pronoun or left in the verb.

article/absence-article/definite/complem.description: if the complement precedes the object, it may be definite

article/absence-article/definite/monadic.description: one-of-a-kind nouns do not need the article to be definite; this applies to nouns that are referentially unique due to modifiers (e.g., adjective [as in πνεῦμα ἅγιον] or genitive [υἱὸς θεοῦ])
article/absence-article/definite/monadic.formation: A noun naming something of which there is only one (the sun, the moon, the earth) left without the article and definite all the same, since its uniqueness identifies it. A phrase made unique by its modifier behaves the same way, so the whole phrase, not the bare noun, is what counts.

article/absence-article/definite/abstrac.description: love, joy, peace, etc. are often anarthrous, but not indefinite
article/absence-article/definite/abstrac.formation: An abstract noun (joy, peace, hope, wisdom) without the article, definite or qualitative rather than indefinite: 'joy', never 'a joy'. The quality itself is in view, and there is often little felt difference from the articular form.

article/absence-article/definite/genitiv.description: anarthrous head noun with anarthrous genitive noun: both usually have the same semantic force (usually definite or qualitative)
article/absence-article/definite/genitiv.formation: A head noun and its dependent genitive noun, both without the article, sharing the same force: usually both definite, sometimes both qualitative, rarely one definite and the other indefinite. The genitive tends to be definite and to make its head definite with it, so the anarthrous pair means much the same as the articular pair.

article/absence-article/definite/pronomi.description: nouns with πᾶς, ὅλος, etc. do not need the article to be definite, for either the class as a whole (“all”) or distributively (“every”) is being specified
article/absence-article/definite/pronomi.formation: A noun with πᾶς or ὅλος and no article, definite because the adjective already sets the extent: 'every —', 'all —', 'the whole —'. The whole class or each member of it is in view, which gives the phrase a generic force.

article/absence-article/definite/generic.description: the whole class is in view; little semantic difference between this and articular generic nouns
article/absence-article/definite/generic.formation: A noun without the article that stands for its whole class: 'a person' meaning people in general, 'slave or free' meaning anyone of either kind. There is little difference in sense from the articular generic; English often uses 'a' or a plural.

article/special-uses-non-uses-article.display_name: Special Uses and Non-Uses of the Article

article/special-uses-non-uses-article/an.display_name: Anarthrous Pre-Verbal Predicate Nominatives (Involving Colwell’s Rule)

article/special-uses-non-uses-article/an.description: a definite predicate nominative that precedes the verb is usually anarthrous
article/special-uses-non-uses-article/an.formation: A definite predicate nominative that stands before the linking verb usually lacks the article, while one after the verb usually has it: word order does the article's work. The subject is marked by the article or is a pronoun, and a genitive on the predicate often makes its definiteness plain. The rule runs one way only: an anarthrous predicate before the verb is more often qualitative than definite.

article/special-uses-non-uses-article/an.description: the converse is not true; anarthrous preverbal PNs are usually qualitative. θεός in John 1:1c is probably qualitative (thus, not identifying the λόγος with the person of ὁ θεός, but stressing that their natures are the same: “What God was, the Word was” [NEB]).

article/special-uses-non-uses-article/ar.display_name: The Article with Multiple Substantives Connected by Καί (Granville Sharp Rule and Related Constructions)
Statement of the Granville Sharp Rule
article/special-uses-non-uses-article/ar.description: both substantives (nouns, participles, adjectives) refer to the same person in the article-substantive-καί-substantive (TSKS) construction when:

article/special-uses-non-uses-article/ar.display_name: Validity of the Rule Within the New Testament
article/special-uses-non-uses-article/ar.description: always valid; Titus 2:13 & 2 Pet 1:1 impacted. Exceptions outside the NT are capable of linguistic explanation and do not affect the christologically significant texts

article/special-uses-non-uses-article/ar.display_name: TSKS Constructions Involving Impersonal, Plural, and Proper Nouns

article/special-uses-non-uses-article/ar.description: always distinct individuals (e.g., “the Peter and James”)
article/special-uses-non-uses-article/ar.formation: One article over two personal names joined by καί, the second without an article: the article groups the two people as a pair that belongs together for the matter at hand, but two names always name two different people.

article/special-uses-non-uses-article/ar.description: three different semantic groups possible: (1) distinct, (2) identical, (3) overlap (three subgroups). This breaks down:
article/special-uses-non-uses-article/ar.formation: One article over two plural personal substantives (nouns, adjectives or participles) joined by καί, the second without its own article. The single article unites the groups, which may be distinct, overlap, one contained in the other, or the same people described two ways; the last is the usual sense when both are participles.

article/special-uses-non-uses-article/ar.description: three different semantic groups possible: (1) distinct, (2) identical, (3) overlap (three subgroups). All are represented, though #2 (identical) is rare. Affects Acts 2:23; 20:21; 2 Thess 2:1; etc.

article/special-uses-non-uses-article/ar.formation: One article governing two or more substantives joined by καί (article–substantive–καί–substantive), the second without an article of its own. The single article groups them as one unit for the matter at hand. With plural, impersonal or proper nouns the two do not name the same referent: they may be distinct but united, overlap, or one may be part of the other.

adjectives/adverbial-use-adjective.display_name: The Adverbial Use of the Adjective

adjectives/independent-substantival-use-.display_name: The Independent or Substantival Use of the Adjective
The Use of the Positive Adjective

adjectives/independent-substantival-use-.formation: A positive adjective where a comparative is meant, comparing two things: 'it is good (= better) for you to… than to…'. The second term follows ἤ, stands in the genitive, or is left to the context; the form is positive and the comparison is carried by the construction.

adjectives/independent-substantival-use-.description: implicit comparison between three or more substantives
adjectives/independent-substantival-use-.formation: A positive adjective meaning 'greatest', 'best', singling one out of three or more. The group is named by a genitive or ἐν, or given by the context, and the article usually marks the one singled out: 'the great (= greatest) commandment'.

The positive form of an adjective (ἀγαθός, μέγας, πιστός), attributing a quality with no comparison: 'a good servant', 'large branches'. Now and then, where the context sets two or more things side by side, the positive form carries a comparative or superlative sense.

adjectives/independent-substantival-use-.display_name: The Use of the Comparative Adjective

adjectives/independent-substantival-use-.description: explicit comparison between two; adjective usually followed by genitive or ἤ
very + positive form of adjective; no comparison is made (thus, ἰσχυρότερος would be very strong rather than stronger)

adjectives/independent-substantival-use-.display_name: The Use of the Superlative Adjective

adjectives/independent-substantival-use-.description: the extreme in a comparison of three or more
very + positive form of the adjective
only two are compared; frequent with πρῶτος, rare with other terms

adjectives/relation-adjective-noun.display_name: The Relation of Adjective to Noun

adjectives/relation-adjective-noun/when-.description: article-adjective-noun (ὁ ἀγαθὸς βασιλεύς = the good king)
article-noun-article-adjective (ὁ βασιλεὺς ὁ ἀγαθός = the good king)
noun-article-adjective (βασιλεὺς ὁ ἀγαθός = the good king) (rare with adjectives, more common with other modifiers)

adjectives/relation-adjective-noun/when-.formation: The adjective stands inside the article-noun group and qualifies the noun. First attributive: article, adjective, noun (ὁ ἀγαθὸς ἄνθρωπος), the commonest. Second: article, noun, article, adjective (ὁ ἄνθρωπος ὁ ἀγαθός), weighting both noun and adjective. Third: noun, article, adjective (ἄνθρωπος ὁ ἀγαθός), the rarest.

adjectives/relation-adjective-noun/when-.description: adjective makes assertion about the noun
adjective-article-noun (ἀγαθὸς ὁ βασιλεύς = the king is good)
article-noun-adjective (ὁ βασιλεὺς ἀγαθός = the king is good)

adjectives/relation-adjective-noun/when-.formation: The adjective stands outside the article-noun group and asserts something of the noun, making a clause of its own: 'the salt is good'. First predicate: adjective, article, noun (ἀγαθὸς ὁ ἄνθρωπος). Second: article, noun, adjective (ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἀγαθός). The copula is often left out.

With an articular noun, the adjective's place relative to the article decides its relation to the noun. Inside the article-noun group (ὁ ἀγαθὸς ἄνθρωπος, ὁ ἄνθρωπος ὁ ἀγαθός) it is attributive and qualifies the noun; outside it (ἀγαθὸς ὁ ἄνθρωπος, ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἀγαθός) it is predicate and asserts something of the noun, with εἰμί expressed or understood.

An anarthrous adjective beside an anarthrous noun, in either order (ἀγαθὸς ἄνθρωπος, ἄνθρωπος ἀγαθός). It is usually attributive ('a wise builder', 'a good work'), but may be predicate ('blessed is the man'), especially where no verb is expressed and the adjective leads; only the context decides.

pronouns/semantic-categories/personal-pr.description: to identify, give prominence to, clarify, etc.; contrast not prominent, though sometimes present
sometimes as a “switch-reference” device, to show alternating subjects; other times, merely stylistic
Anaphoric: to stand in the place of a noun or other nominal

pronouns/semantic-categories/personal-pr.formation: The genitive of a personal pronoun marking possession: 'her old age', 'his house', 'our word'. Unemphatic, it follows its articular noun (ὁ λόγος ἡμῶν, the enclitic μου, σου); set before the article-noun group, or in the accented form ἐμοῦ, σοῦ, it stresses the owner.

A personal pronoun in an oblique case used where a reflexive (ἐμαυτοῦ, σεαυτοῦ, ἑαυτοῦ) would be expected, pointing back to the subject of its own clause: 'store up for yourselves', 'she glorified herself'. Nothing in the form marks it; the context shows that the pronoun refers to the subject.

ἐγώ, σύ (with their plurals) and αὐτός. Since the verb already carries person, a nominative pronoun is not needed, and when present it usually marks emphasis or contrast: 'you have kept…', 'am I not…?'. In the oblique cases the pronoun simply stands for the person or thing. αὐτός is 'he', 'she', 'it' in the oblique cases; in the nominative it is often 'he himself'.

pronouns/semantic-categories/demonstrati.description: οὗτος and ἐκεῖνος sometimes have diminished demonstrative force; equivalent to third person personal pronouns
unnecessary use, sometimes for rhetorical effect

pronouns/semantic-categories/demonstrati.display_name: Constructio ad Sensum (construction according to sense)
pronouns/semantic-categories/demonstrati.description: natural gender or number is used instead of grammatical gender or number (as in τὰ ἔθνη … οὗτοι [“the Gentiles … these”])
lack of concord in gender between pronoun and antecedent
lack of concord in number between pronoun and antecedent
neuter of οὗτος routinely used to refer to a phrase or clause

pronouns/semantic-categories/demonstrati.formation: οὗτος points to what is near, in the scene or in the text just said, and ἐκεῖνος to what is farther off; ὅδε, rare, points forward to what follows. With a noun they take the predicate position (οὗτος ὁ ἄνθρωπος, ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἐκεῖνος); alone they stand for a person or thing, or for a whole idea ('this', 'that', 'for this reason').

pronouns/semantic-categories/relative-pr.description: ὅς and ὅστις labeled relative pronouns because they relate to more than one clause
link a substantive to the relative clause, which either describes, clarifies, or restricts the meaning of the substantive
“glitch” in concord, identification of antecedent, etc.

pronouns/semantic-categories/relative-pr.display_name: Natural Gender vs. Grammatical Gender (constructio ad sensum)

pronouns/semantic-categories/relative-pr.description: attracted to the case of the antecedent
antecedent attracted to the case of the RP

pronouns/semantic-categories/relative-pr.formation: A relative pronoun whose case is not the one its own clause requires. In attraction, the commoner kind, a relative that should be accusative takes the genitive or dative of its antecedent: ἐν ὥρᾳ ᾗ for ἐν ὥρᾳ ἥν, 'in an hour which'. In inverse attraction, rarer, the antecedent is drawn into the case of the relative.

pronouns/semantic-categories/relative-pr.description: due to embedded demonstrative or poetry
after a preposition; adverbial/conjunctive force; no antecedent, or antecedent is conceptual
focuses on the whole class (thus, whoever = everyone who)
focuses on the nature or essence of the person or thing in view (the very one who, who certainly, who indeed)

pronouns/semantic-categories/relative-pr.formation: ὅς (and ὅστις) opens a clause describing a word in another clause. It agrees with that antecedent in gender and number, but its case comes from its role in its own clause: 'my child, whom I fathered'. ὅστις generalizes or characterizes ('whoever', 'the kind who'). The antecedent may be left unexpressed: 'whoever has'.

pronouns/semantic-categories/interrogati.description: asks identifying question (Who? What?) in direct and indirect questions. Sometimes τίς asks What sort? (qualitative), and τί asks Why? (adverbial).
asks qualitative (What sort?) and quantitative question (How much?), respectively.

pronouns/semantic-categories/indefinite-.description: introduces a member of a class without further identification (τις, τι)

pronouns/semantic-categories/possessive-.description: no distinct form in Greek, but (348):

pronouns/semantic-categories/possessive-.display_name: Possessive Adjective (ἐμός, σός, ἡμέτερος, ὑμέτερος) lexicalizes possession
Personal Pronoun in Genitive (αὐτοῦ) grammaticalizes possession

pronouns/semantic-categories/intensive-p.description: himself, herself, itself (in predicate position to an articular noun)
same (modifying an articular substantive in the attributive position)

pronouns/semantic-categories/intensive-p.display_name: As a Third Person Personal Pronoun

pronouns/semantic-categories/reflexive-p.description: ἐμαυτοῦ (of myself), σεαυτοῦ (of yourself), ἑαυτοῦ (of himself), ἑαυτῶν (of themselves); used to highlight the participation of the subject in the verbal action, as direct object, indirect object, intensifier, etc.

pronouns/semantic-categories/reciprocal-.description: ἀλλήλων (of one another) used to indicate an interchange between two or more groups; thus, always plural

prepositions/ἀνά-accusative/distributive.description: in the midst of (ἀνὰ μέσον + G); each, apiece (with numbers)

prepositions/ἀνά-accusative.formation: ἀνά with the accusative, rare as a free preposition: in the phrase ἀνὰ μέσον with a genitive, 'in the midst of', 'between'; and distributively, 'each', 'apiece', 'at a time', often with a number or a word of measure. Its sense of 'up' survives mostly in compound verbs.

prepositions/ἀντί-genitive/exchange-equi.description: for, as, in the place of

prepositions/ἀντί-genitive.formation: ἀντί with the genitive: 'instead of', 'in place of' (substitution), and 'in return for', 'for' (exchange), the two often blending; occasionally 'because of' (ἀνθ' ὧν, ἀντὶ τούτου). One thing takes the place of, or is traded for, another.

prepositions/ἀπό-genitive/partitive-i-e-.display_name: Partitive (i.e., substituting for a partitive gen.)

prepositions/ἀπό-genitive.formation: ἀπό with the genitive, 'from', 'away from': separation from a place or person; also source ('from'), time from which ('from … on'), cause ('because of'), and in place of a partitive genitive ('one of', 'some of'). It overlaps with ἐκ, which is narrower, 'out of'.

prepositions/διά-genitive-accusative/acc.description: because of, on account of, for the sake of

prepositions/διά-genitive-accusative.formation: διά with two cases. With the genitive: 'through', of passing through a place or a stretch of time, and of the intermediate agent or the means by which something is done. With the accusative: 'because of', 'on account of', giving the cause or reason.

prepositions/εἰς-accusative/result.description: so that, with the result that

prepositions/εἰς-accusative/reference-re.description: with respect to, with reference to

prepositions/εἰς-accusative/place-ἐν-its.display_name: In the place of ἐν (with its various nuances)
prepositions/εἰς-accusative/place-ἐν-its.formation: εἰς used where ἐν would be expected, for position rather than movement: 'in', 'at', 'on'. It happens chiefly with verbs of rest (κάθημαι, εἰμί, τηρέω), whose stative sense overrides the motion εἰς normally carries; the phrase then means where something is, not where it is going.

prepositions/εἰς-accusative.formation: εἰς with the accusative, basically movement 'into' or 'toward': of place ('into', 'to'), of time ('for', 'until'), and figuratively of goal, purpose or result ('for', 'so as to'), reference ('with regard to'), advantage ('for') or hostility ('against'). With a verb of rest it can mean simply 'in'.

prepositions/ἐκ-genitive.description: from, out of, away from, of

prepositions/ἐκ-genitive/partitive-i-e-s.display_name: Partitive (i.e., substituting for a partitive gen.)

prepositions/ἐκ-genitive.formation: ἐκ with the genitive, 'out of', 'from': movement out of a place or group, and source or origin; also time from which ('since', 'from … on'), cause or means ('by', 'because of'), manner ('out of', e.g. out of reluctance), and in place of a partitive genitive ('one of').

prepositions/ἐν-dative/thing-possessed.description: with (in the sense of which possesses)

prepositions/ἐν-dative/as-equivalent-for.display_name: As an equivalent for εἰς (with verbs of motion)

prepositions/ἐπί-genitive-dative-accusat.description: at, at the time of, during
on, upon, to, up to, against

prepositions/ἐπί-genitive-dative-accusat.formation: ἐπί with three cases, basically 'on', 'upon'. With the genitive: position 'on', 'at', 'before', and 'in the time of'. With the dative: 'on', 'at', and the ground or occasion, 'at', 'because of' (amazed at…). With the accusative: motion 'onto', 'to', 'against', and a stretch of time, 'for'.

prepositions/κατά-genitive-accusative/ac.description: “indicating the division of a greater whole into individual parts”
with respect to, with reference to

prepositions/κατά-genitive-accusative.formation: κατά with two cases, basically 'down'. With the genitive: 'down from', 'throughout', and 'against'. With the accusative: 'according to', the standard something follows; 'along', 'throughout' a place; 'at' a time; and distributively, 'each', 'by' (every year, house by house).

prepositions/μετά-genitive-accusative.formation: μετά with two cases. With the genitive: 'with', of company or accompaniment, and of the manner or circumstance an action goes with (with joy, with haste). With the accusative: 'after', of time.

prepositions/παρά-genitive-dative-accusa.description: in general, from (the side of) (with a personal object)

prepositions/παρά-genitive-dative-accusa.formation: παρά with three cases, basically 'beside'. With the genitive, almost always of a person: 'from (the side of)', of source or agency. With the dative: 'beside', 'with', 'in the presence of'. With the accusative: 'alongside', 'by' a place, and figuratively 'more than' or 'contrary to'.

prepositions/περί-genitive-accusative.formation: περί with two cases, basically 'around'. With the genitive: 'about', 'concerning', and at times 'for', 'on behalf of'. With the accusative: 'around' a place or person, and 'about' a time.

prepositions/πρό-genitive.formation: πρό with the genitive, 'before': in front of a place, earlier than a time (with a stretch of time, 'so long before'), and in rank or importance ('above all').

prepositions/πρός-accusative-almost-excl.description: so that, with the result that
with, in company with (with stative verbs)

prepositions/πρός-accusative-almost-excl.formation: πρός almost always with the accusative, basically 'toward', facing: movement 'to', 'toward'; position 'at', 'by' (at the door); speech 'to'; a length of time, 'for (a while)'; and figuratively purpose or result ('for', 'leading to'), association ('with') and opposition ('against').

prepositions/σύν-dative.description: Expresses accompaniment/association: with, in association (company) with
prepositions/σύν-dative.formation: σύν with the dative, 'with', 'together with': accompaniment or association, especially of people who belong together; also of things added together ('along with'). It is close to μετά with the genitive.

prepositions/ὑπέρ-genitive-accusative/ge.description: on behalf of, for the sake of
in place of, instead of (= ἀντί) (such instances also involve representation)

prepositions/ὑπέρ-genitive-accusative.formation: ὑπέρ with two cases, basically 'over', 'above'. With the genitive: 'for', 'on behalf of', 'for the sake of' (the one who benefits), shading into 'in place of'; also 'concerning'. With the accusative: 'above', 'beyond', 'more than', of what surpasses something else.

prepositions/ὑπό-genitive-accusative.formation: ὑπό with two cases, basically 'under'. With the genitive: 'by', the agent, usually after a passive verb. With the accusative: 'under', 'beneath' a place, and 'under' authority or control.

person-number.description: Usual examples of concord are not covered in this chapter; the following are, for the most part, unusual & exegetically significant uses.

person-number/person/first-person-for-th.description: for the sake of vividness when a more universal application is in view

person-number/person/first-person-plural.description: first person plural by an author when he is only speaking about himself
first person plural includes both author(s) and audience
first person plural restricts the group to the author and his associates

person-number/number/neuter-plural-subje.display_name: Neuter Plural Subject with Singular Verb
person-number/number/neuter-plural-subje.description: neuter plural subjects normally take singular verbs since impersonal things are usually in view; treated as a collective whole; when they take a plural verb, individual identity is stressed

person-number/number/collective-singular.display_name: Collective Singular Subject with Plural Verb
person-number/number/collective-singular.description: when words such as ὄχλος take plural verb, individual identity is stressed

person-number/number/compound-subject-si.description: first-named subject is stressed (e.g., “Jesus and the disciples comes”)

person-number/number/indefinite-plural.description: “They” = “Someone” (convert plural into a passive in which the object becomes the subject; “Have they discovered a cure for cancer?” = “Has a cure for cancer been discovered?”)

person-number/number/categorical-plural-.description: “They” = “He, She” (like indefinite plural, but can be used with plural nouns); focuses more on action than actor

voice.description: indicates how subject is related to the action [or state] expressed by the verb

voice/active.description: Subject performs, produces, or experiences the action or exists in the state expressed by the verb

voice/active/simple-active.description: subject performs or experiences the action
voice/active/simple-active.formation: An active verb whose subject performs the action, or experiences it, with or without a direct object: the ordinary use of the voice. The subject is the doer, and the verb says nothing special about the subject's involvement.

voice/active/causative-active-k-ergative.description: subject is not directly involved in the action, but is the ultimate source of it
voice/active/causative-active-k-ergative.formation: An active verb whose subject does not carry out the action himself but is its source or cause: 'the governor flogged him' when he had him flogged, 'I watered' when I gave the plants to drink. Many verbs in -όω and -ίζω are causative in themselves; with others only the context shows that someone else did the deed.

voice/active/stative-active.description: subject exists in the state indicated by the verb
voice/active/stative-active.formation: An active verb whose subject simply exists in a state rather than doing anything: the linking verbs, and verbs that English renders 'to be' plus an adjective ('to be rich', 'to be patient', 'to be angry').

voice/active/reflexive-active.description: active verb + reflexive pronoun (subject acts upon himself or herself)
voice/active/reflexive-active.formation: An active verb with a reflexive pronoun (ἑαυτόν, σεαυτόν, ἐμαυτόν) as its object, so that the subject acts on itself: 'he tied it round himself', 'whoever humbles himself'. Koine increasingly uses this where earlier Greek used the direct middle.

voice/middle.description: Subject performs or experiences the action expressed by the verb in such a way that emphasizes the subject’s participation; subject acts with a vested interest

voice/middle/direct-middle-k-reflexive-d.display_name: Direct Middle (a.k.a. Reflexive or Direct Reflexive)
voice/middle/direct-middle-k-reflexive-d.description: verb + self (as direct object); subject acts on himself or herself
voice/middle/direct-middle-k-reflexive-d.formation: A middle verb whose subject acts directly on itself, as if 'himself' were its object, with no pronoun: 'he clothed himself', 'he was warming himself', 'he will gird himself'. It is rare in the New Testament, found mostly with verbs of dressing, washing and the like; elsewhere the active with a reflexive pronoun has taken its place.

voice/middle/redundant-middle.description: the use of the middle voice in a reflexive manner with a reflexive pronoun

voice/middle/indirect-middle-k-indirect-.display_name: Indirect Middle (a.k.a. Indirect Reflexive, Benefactive, Intensive, Dynamic)
voice/middle/indirect-middle-k-indirect-.description: subject acts for (or sometimes by) himself or herself, or in his or her own interest; key: like active verb + reflexive pronoun in dative
voice/middle/indirect-middle-k-indirect-.formation: A middle verb whose subject acts for itself, in its own interest, or with special involvement, as if 'for himself' were added: 'they picked out the best places for themselves', 'he kept back part of the price for himself'. The verb usually has its own object; the middle points the action back to the subject's benefit.

voice/middle/causative-middle.description: subject has something done for or to himself or herself

voice/middle/permissive-middle.description: subject allows something to be done for or to himself or herself
voice/middle/permissive-middle.formation: A middle verb whose subject allows or arranges for something to be done to or for itself, without doing it personally: 'to get oneself registered', 'to have one's head shaved'. It reads like a passive, but adds the subject's consent or initiative.

voice/middle/reciprocal-middle.description: verb with plural subject to represent interaction among themselves

voice/middle/deponent-middle.description: generally, no active form but active meaning; specifically, no active form for a particular principal part in Hellenistic Greek, and one whose force in that principal part is evidently active
voice/middle/deponent-middle.formation: A verb middle in form but active in meaning, with no active form in that tense: ἔρχομαι, δύναμαι, ἐργάζομαι, πορεύομαι, βούλομαι, and futures such as λήμψομαι. It is translated as an ordinary active; whether some middle sense lingers is debated, so it is best used of verbs that are plainly active in meaning.

voice/passive.description: The subject is acted upon or receives the action expressed by the verb

voice/passive/passive-constructions/pass.display_name: The Passive With and Without Expressed Agency

voice/passive/passive-constructions/pass.description: usually ὑπό (+ gen.), sometimes ἀπό (+ gen.) or παρά (+ gen.), indicating the person who is ultimately responsible for the action
διά (+ gen.), indicating the person who carries out the act for the ultimate agent
ἐν (+ dat.), simple dative, or sometimes ἐκ (+ gen.), indicating the means an agent uses to perform an act

various reasons why agency is unexpressed (such as: obvious from context, focus on subject, nature of some verbs requires none, equative verbs, implicit generic agent, obtrusiveness of an explicit agent, rhetorical effect; divine passive is not a separate category, but may belong to several of the previous ones)

especially with accusative of thing (in person-thing double accusative construction) as a retained object; thing stays as accusative when verb becomes passive; person becomes subject (e.g., “She taught you the lesson” becomes “You were taught the lesson by her”)

voice/passive/passive-uses/simple-passiv.formation: A passive verb whose subject receives the action, with no suggestion of the subject's consent or cause. The agent may be named (ὑπό with the genitive for the person, διά with the genitive for an intermediary, the dative or ἐν for the means) or left unstated.

voice/passive/passive-uses/causative-per.description: implies consent, permission, or cause of the action of the verb on the part of the subject receiving the action

voice/passive/passive-uses/deponent-pass.description: generally, no active form but active meaning; specifically, no active form for a particular principal part in Hellenistic Greek, and one whose force in that principal part is evidently active
voice/passive/passive-uses/deponent-pass.formation: A verb passive in form but active in meaning, with no active form in that tense: the aorists ἀπεκρίθην ('I answered'), ἐγενήθην, ἐπορεύθην, ἐφοβήθην and the like. It is translated as an active; nobody acts on the subject.

moods.description: present [the speaker’s portrayal of his affirmation of certainty of] the verbal action or state with reference to its actuality or potentiality

moods/indicative.description: The mood of assertion, or presentation of certainty

moods/indicative/declarative-indicative.description: presents assertion as a noncontingent (or unqualified) statement
moods/indicative/declarative-indicative.formation: An indicative that simply asserts something as so: a plain, unqualified statement, whether or not it is true. It is the ordinary use of the mood, with no condition, question or command attached.

moods/indicative/interrogative-indicativ.description: question of fact; expects a declarative indicative in response
moods/indicative/interrogative-indicativ.formation: An indicative in a question of fact, asking what, who, where or whether, and expecting a statement in reply. An interrogative word (τίς, ποῦ, πόθεν) or particle often marks it; the deliberative subjunctive asks instead what ought to be done or whether something is possible.

moods/indicative/conditional-indicative.description: indicative with εἰ in protasis—first class: assumed true for sake of argument; second class: assumed false (for sake of argument)
moods/indicative/conditional-indicative.formation: An indicative with εἰ in the 'if' clause of a condition. With εἰ and any tense the condition is assumed true for the argument's sake (first class): 'if you do this, and suppose you do, then…'. With εἰ and a past tense, and ἄν in the 'then' clause, it is assumed untrue (second class): 'if you had…, you would have…'.

moods/indicative/potential-indicative.description: semantically equivalent to a potential mood, due to verbal root; found in verbs of obligation, wish, or desire (such as ὀφείλω, δεῖ, θέλω), followed by infinitive
moods/indicative/potential-indicative.formation: An indicative of a verb of obligation, wish or desire (δεῖ, ὀφείλω, βούλομαι, θέλω) followed by an infinitive: 'we ought to…', 'I want you to…'. The verb asserts the obligation or the wish; the action itself, in the infinitive, remains only potential.

moods/indicative/cohortative-command-vol.description: future indicative is sometimes used for a command

moods/indicative/indicative-ὃτι/substant.description: functions as direct object of verb
direct object of a transitive verb that is not a verb of perception

moods/indicative/indicative-ὃτι/substant.display_name: Direct Discourse (a.k.a. Recitative Ὃτι Clause, Ὃτι Recitativum)
moods/indicative/indicative-ὃτι/substant.description: after verb of perception; in place of ὅτι, put in quotation marks
after verb of perception; ὅτι clause contains reported speech or thought; translation: that

moods/indicative/indicative-ὃτι/substant.display_name: Apposition (to noun, pronoun, or other substantive)
moods/indicative/indicative-ὃτι/substant.description: namely, that (can be substituted for its antecedent)

moods/indicative/indicative-ὃτι/epexeget.description: explains or clarifies or completes a previous word or phrase (similar to apposition, but cannot be substituted for its antecedent)
moods/indicative/indicative-ὃτι/epexeget.formation: A ὅτι clause with the indicative that explains, clarifies or completes a preceding word or phrase, often a question or a verb of noticing: 'to the effect that', 'in that'. Unlike an appositional ὅτι clause, it cannot stand in place of the word it explains.

moods/indicative/indicative-ὃτι/causal-a.formation: A ὅτι clause with the indicative giving the reason for the main clause: 'because', 'for'. It gives the reason, not the content, so its tenses are rendered normally rather than shifted back as in reported speech.

moods/subjunctive.description: Generally represents the verbal action (or state) as uncertain but probable; however, since it encroaches on the optative’s domain in Koine, it has broadened out to include possible, hypothetical, and impossible

moods/subjunctive/independent-clauses/ho.display_name: Hortatory Subjunctive (a.k.a. Volitive; but this also means imperatival)
moods/subjunctive/independent-clauses/ho.description: let us (first person plural used to exhort oneself and one’s associates); rarely, first person singular is used (let me)
moods/subjunctive/independent-clauses/ho.formation: A first person plural subjunctive urging the speaker and others to act together: 'let us…'. Rarely it is first person singular, 'let me…', usually after ἄφες or δεῦρο. It fills the place of a first person imperative, which Greek lacks.

moods/subjunctive/independent-clauses/de.description: asks either a real or rhetorical question; a hortatory subjunctive turned into a question; asks about possibility, necessity, or moral obligation
moods/subjunctive/independent-clauses/de.formation: A subjunctive, usually first person, in a question about what should or can be done: 'which road should we take?', 'should we sell the ox or not?'. A real question looks for an answer about possibility or means; a rhetorical one is a disguised statement of what ought to be. It asks about oughtness, not fact.

moods/subjunctive/independent-clauses/em.description: οὐ μή plus the aorist subjunctive (strong negation, not even possible)
moods/subjunctive/independent-clauses/em.formation: οὐ μή with the aorist subjunctive, less often the future indicative: the strongest denial Greek has, 'will never', 'will certainly not'. It rules out even the possibility, and usually speaks of the future.

moods/subjunctive/independent-clauses/pr.description: usually μή + aorist subjunctive, typically in the second person; equivalent to μή + imperative: Do not (rather than You should not)
moods/subjunctive/independent-clauses/pr.formation: μή with the aorist subjunctive, usually second person, as a negative command: 'do not…'. It forbids the action as a whole, and is the normal second person prohibition with the aorist, since Greek does not use μή with the second person aorist imperative.

moods/subjunctive/dependent-subordinate-.description: subjunctive with ἐάν in protasis—third class condition (may indicate more probable future, mere possibility, or hypothetical situation); fifth class condition (a.k.a. present general condition) (indicates a generic situation in the present time)
moods/subjunctive/dependent-subordinate-.formation: A subjunctive with ἐάν in the 'if' clause of a condition, whose 'then' clause may be in almost any mood or tense. With a future or a command it states a likely, possible or hypothetical future case (third class); with a present indicative it states what holds generally, 'whenever this happens, that follows' (fifth class).

moods/subjunctive/dependent-subordinate-.display_name: Purpose Ἳνα Clause (a.k.a. Final or Telic Ἳνα)
moods/subjunctive/dependent-subordinate-.description: in order that, so that (indicates the purpose or intention of the controlling verb)

moods/subjunctive/dependent-subordinate-.display_name: Result Ἳνα Clause (a.k.a. Consecutive or Ecbatic Ἳνα)
moods/subjunctive/dependent-subordinate-.description: so that, with the result that (indicates a consequence of the verbal action that is not intended)
indicates both the intention and its sure accomplishment
ἵνα clause indicates some substantival function

moods/subjunctive/dependent-subordinate-.display_name: Direct Object Clause (a.k.a. Content Ἳνα Clause)

moods/subjunctive/dependent-subordinate-.description: after a noun or adjective to explain or clarify that noun or adjective
completes the meaning of a helping verb such as θέλω, δύναμαι (total verbal meaning is usually purpose)
equal to a command (could be treated as an independent use of subjunctive since the ἵνα clause is not subordinate to a main verb)
μή plus the subjunctive can be used after verbs of fearing, warning, watching out for to serve as a warning
moods/subjunctive/dependent-subordinate-.formation: μή (or μήποτε, μή πως) with the subjunctive after a verb of fearing, warning or watching out (φοβέομαι, βλέπω), naming what might happen: 'lest', 'that … not'. It warns, or voices anxiety about a possible outcome.

moods/subjunctive/dependent-subordinate-.description: follows the main verb, but appears awkward in the sentence structure (reflects a deliberative subjunctive from the direct question)
moods/subjunctive/dependent-subordinate-.formation: A deliberative subjunctive kept inside a reported question after a main verb such as ἔχω, οἶδα or μεριμνάω, with an interrogative word: 'he did not know where to go' (literally, 'where he should go'). It sits awkwardly in the sentence and is smoothed out in translation.

moods/subjunctive/dependent-subordinate-.description: after ὅστις (ἄν/ἐάν) or ὅς (δʼ) ἄν; construction indicates a generic or indefinite subject; translate like an indicative (since the contingency is of the person, not the action)
moods/subjunctive/dependent-subordinate-.formation: A relative clause with ὃς ἄν (ὃς ἐάν) or ὅστις and the subjunctive, with a generic or indefinite subject: 'whoever…', 'whatever…'. The uncertainty lies in who does it, not in the action, so it is translated like an indicative; it works much like a condition.

moods/subjunctive/dependent-subordinate-.description: after a temporal adverb (or improper preposition) meaning until (e.g., ἕως, ἄχρι, μέχρι) or whenever (ὅταν), indicating a future contingency
moods/subjunctive/dependent-subordinate-.formation: A temporal clause with the subjunctive after ὅταν ('whenever') or a word meaning 'until' (ἕως, ἄχρι, μέχρι, often with ἄν or οὗ). It marks a future or indefinite contingency, measured from the time of the main verb.

moods/optative.description: Generally portrays an action as possible

moods/optative/voluntative-optative-k-op.display_name: Voluntative Optative (a.k.a. Optative of Obtainable Wish, Volitive Optative)
moods/optative/voluntative-optative-k-op.description: expresses an obtainable wish or a prayer (e.g., μὴ γένοιτο—may it never be!)
moods/optative/voluntative-optative-k-op.formation: An optative in an independent clause expressing a wish or prayer that can be fulfilled: 'may…'. It is common in blessings and greetings, and in the fixed phrase μὴ γένοιτο, 'may it never be!', rejecting a wrong conclusion.

moods/optative/oblique-optative.description: used in indirect questions after a secondary tense (substitutes for an indicative or subjunctive of the direct question)
moods/optative/oblique-optative.formation: An optative in an indirect question after a past tense verb of asking or wondering, standing for the indicative or subjunctive of the direct question: 'the guard asked what the noise might be'. It is literary, and found only in Luke's writings.

moods/optative/potential-optative.description: with the particle ἄν in the apodosis of an incomplete fourth class condition; protasis needs to be supplied (e.g., [If he could do something,] he would do this)
moods/optative/potential-optative.formation: An optative with ἄν in the 'then' part of an unstated, unlikely condition: 'what would he…?', 'how could I…?'. The 'if' clause has to be supplied in thought, and the whole is polite or doubtful.

moods/optative/conditional-optative.description: in the protasis of a fourth class condition (with εἰ) to indicate remote possibility (e.g., if he could do something, if perhaps this should occur)
moods/optative/conditional-optative.formation: An optative with εἰ in the 'if' clause of a condition presented as a remote possibility: 'if perhaps…', 'if it should…'. The New Testament never completes it with an optative 'then' clause; the main clause is left to be supplied or is in another mood.

moods/imperative.description: The mood of intention (in the realm of volition rather than cognition)

moods/imperative/command.description: commands an action to be done, usually from a superior to an inferior in rank
moods/imperative/command.formation: An imperative directing someone to act, usually from a superior to someone under them: second person 'do this', third person 'he must…' (often rendered 'let him…'). The aorist commands the action as a whole; the present commands it as an ongoing process or practice.

moods/imperative/prohibition.description: μή + imperative; forbids an action, usually from a superior to an inferior in rank
moods/imperative/prohibition.formation: μή with an imperative, almost always present, forbidding an action: 'do not…', and in the third person 'he must not…'. The present portrays the forbidden action as a practice or process; to forbid with the aorist in the second person, the subjunctive is used instead.

moods/imperative/request-k-entreaty-poli.description: used to make a request rather than a demand, especially from an inferior in rank to a superior
